Fanyu Meng opens with a personal note. Two years after Ziyu Acoustics gave up its fortnightly schedule, he spends much of his free time on guitar and music (on his video channel Ziyu FM), at the gym and on the squash court. Three years of regular posts had drained what he knew, and readers who went into acoustics because of the account make him want to write again only once he has more to offer. Meanwhile, idling before Christmas, he posts this article in the original English and leaves the translating to ChatGPT and his readers.

Kenneth Ward explains, without mathematics, how delay can be used to manage phase in a car. He builds up from amplitude, wavelength and phase, which he distinguishes from polarity. Two identical waves add up to +6 dB when aligned, lose 3 dB of that at 90° and cancel almost completely at 180°. Whenever the same sound arrives by two paths (left and right, front and rear, both drivers of a crossover, or a reflection), the result is a comb filter: a 27-inch (2 ms) path difference produces deep notches at 250, 750 and 1,250 Hz.

Distance-based delay removes these cancellations for one seat, and the measurements need to be accurate, not ultra-precise. It cannot fix bad source signals, crossover errors, wiring mistakes or reflections. His best practices: check and correct the phase and timing of the incoming (especially factory) signal first, catch wiring errors, set crossovers carefully, and avoid speaker locations that create extra reflections.

Shared by Fanyu Meng from a LinkedIn article by Kenneth Ward (December 2023). Read the original.
